c.tagline: Costa del Sol capital of Picasso, tapas, and sun-soaked beaches.

taxi.fareNote: Málaga taxis are white with a blue stripe and run on the meter; fixed fares apply on set airport and port routes, shown on a posted tariff card.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, ambulance, and fire in English and other languages.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing in the historic centre and on the seafront in season

hood_desc: The walkable old town around the cathedral, Calle Marqués de Larios, the Roman theatre, and the Alcazaba fortress; best for first-timers who want the sights, shops, and tapas bars all on foot.
The 'Barrio de las Artes' between the centre and the port, packed with street-art murals, galleries, the Centre Pompidou, and hip cafes; suits creative travellers who like an arty, design-led base.
Málaga's classic city beach neighbourhood east of the port, lined with the promenade, chiringuito fish shacks, the bullring, and seafront hotels; ideal for a sun-and-sand stay steps from the sand.

The practical district around María Zambrano station and the leafy Ensanche grid, well connected by train and metro with mid-range hotels; a convenient, good-value base for exploring the wider Costa del Sol.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: EMT bus single rides cost about €1.40 in cash, with a rechargeable 'Tarjeta EMT' cutting the fare on multiple journeys. The metro's two lines take contactless bank cards straight at the gate (about €1.35 a ride), and Cercanías suburban trains are paid at station machines. A day travelcard is around €4.
transit.hours: The metro runs roughly 6:30am to 11pm (later on Fridays and Saturdays); EMT buses run through the evening, with a handful of weekend night lines covering the small-hours gap.

transit.m: Cercanías C-1 train to Málaga Centro/María Zambrano, ~12 min
EMT Airport Express (Línea A) to Alameda Principal, ~20-25 min

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% for good service in restaurants is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Espetos de sardinas
food.desc: Sardines threaded on cane skewers and grilled over olive-wood embers in a beached boat; best from May to October.

places.name: El Tintero
places.note: No menu - waiters walk the terrace shouting dishes and you raise a hand.

places.name: Chiringuito El Cachalote
places.note: Classic beach shack on the old fishing seafront; espetos plus fresh catch.

places.name: La Chancla
places.note: Calmer beachfront option with the same fire-grilled sardines.

food.name: Fritura malaguena
food.desc: Mixed fry of anchovies, squid and small fish in a light chickpea-flour coating; it should crack, never feel greasy.

places.name: Los Mellizos
places.note: Long-running seafood house with several city sites; fry-ups done properly.

places.name: Mercado de Atarazanas bars
places.note: Counter bars inside the market fry whatever came off the boats that morning.

places.name: Chiringuito El Cachalote
places.note: Beachside boquerones and calamares with your feet almost in the sand.

food.name: Porra antequerana
food.desc: Thicker, richer cousin of gazpacho - tomato, bread, garlic and olive oil blended cold and topped with ham and egg.

places.name: Mesón Mariano
places.note: Andalusian home cooking near the market; also famed for its artichokes.

places.name: El Pimpi
places.note: Cavernous 18th-century bodega below the Alcazaba; classic Malaga carte.

places.name: La Tranca
places.note: Loud, cheap and locals-first tapas bar with a proper porra in season.

food.name: Boquerones en vinagre and ensalada malaguena
food.desc: Anchovies cured in vinegar and garlic, and a cold salad of salt cod, orange, potato and olives - Malaga's summer tapas.

places.name: La Tranca
places.note: Standing-room bar where the boquerones come with a glass of vermouth.

places.name: Casa Lola
places.note: Bright tiled tapas bar with quick service and generous plates.

places.name: Mercado de Atarazanas
places.note: Buy them by weight from the stalls or eat at the market bars.

food.name: Berenjenas con miel de cana
food.desc: Aubergine sliced thin, fried crisp and finished with dark sugar-cane molasses from the Malaga coast; sweet and salty at once.

places.name: El Mesón de Cervantes
places.note: Argentine-run Andalusian kitchen with strong reviews and small plates.

places.name: El Pimpi
places.note: On the menu year-round in the city's best-known bodega.

places.name: Mesón Mariano
places.note: Traditional version alongside the porra and fried fish.

food.name: Churros con chocolate
food.desc: Thin looping churros fried fresh and dipped in thick chocolate; the Malaga breakfast, taken any time before noon.

places.name: Casa Aranda
places.note: Churreria since 1932 spread across an alley of small rooms; always queueing.

places.name: Cafe Central
places.note: Historic cafe on the main square, and origin of Malaga's coffee-strength scale.

food.name: Vino dulce de Malaga
food.desc: Sweet Pedro Ximenez and Moscatel from the Montes de Malaga, drawn straight from barrels and chalked up on the bar.

places.name: Antigua Casa de Guardia
places.note: Open since 1840; wine from the cask, your tab chalked on the counter.

places.name: El Pimpi
places.note: Barrels signed by visiting celebrities and a full run of Malaga wines.

places.name: La Tranca
places.note: Cheap glasses of sweet Malaga wine with the tapas and loud music.

food.name: Cafe malagueno
food.desc: Malaga orders coffee by its own nine-name scale of milk-to-coffee ratio - nube, sombra, mitad, solo and the rest.

places.name: Cafe Central
places.note: Where the naming system was invented; the chart is on the wall.

places.name: Casa Aranda
places.note: Order a mitad to go with the churros like everyone else.

landmarks: Alcazaba de Málaga
A magnificently preserved Moorish fortress-palace overlooking the city, with terraced gardens, horseshoe arches, and sea views.
Castillo de Gibralfaro
A hilltop 14th-century castle connected to the Alcazaba, prized for offering the single best panoramic view of Málaga and its bay.
Catedral de Málaga (La Manquita)
A Renaissance cathedral nicknamed 'the one-armed lady' for its unfinished second tower, dominating the historic skyline.
Museo Picasso Málaga
Housed in a 16th-century palace, this museum celebrates the city's most famous native son with an extensive collection of his work.
Roman Theatre (Teatro Romano)
A 1st-century BC Roman theatre unearthed at the foot of the Alcazaba, a striking juxtaposition of ancient and Moorish history.
Calle Marqués de Larios
Málaga's elegant, marble-paved main shopping street, especially dazzling when decked out in festive overhead lights.
Centre Pompidou Málaga (El Cubo)
A colorful glass cube on the harborfront housing a branch of the famed Paris modern art museum, a striking piece of contemporary architecture.
Muelle Uno
A modern waterfront promenade and marina lined with palm trees, shops, and views of superyachts against the historic port.
Plaza de Toros de La Malagueta
A striking neo-Mudéjar bullring from 1874, one of Spain's oldest and most photogenic, with a circular colonnaded facade.
Playa de la Malagueta
Málaga's golden city beach, a lively stretch of sand backed by palm-lined promenades right next to the historic centre.

train.note: No cross-border trains run from Málaga. AVE high-speed services from María Zambrano station reach Madrid in about 2h30 and Barcelona in 5h45, with Avant and media-distancia trains to Córdoba and Seville; for France you change at Barcelona Sants. The C-1 Cercanías line runs along the coast to Torremolinos, Benalmádena and Fuengirola and calls at the airport. Renfe opens booking around 60 days ahead and the cheap Promo fares go first.

bus.note: Coaches use the Estación de Autobuses next to María Zambrano station. ALSA's Morocco services cross by ferry at the Strait of Gibraltar and take well over a day - carry your passport. Domestically ALSA runs constantly along the Costa del Sol to Marbella, Nerja and Ronda, and inland to Granada in about 1h45.

ferry.note: Málaga's ferry terminal is at the port a short walk from the centre. Sailings go to the Spanish enclave of Melilla on the Moroccan coast rather than to Morocco itself, so it is domestic travel but a useful land gateway into Morocco once you arrive. Crossings are mostly overnight; book a cabin in summer and well ahead if taking a car. The port also handles a heavy cruise trade.

half.name: Ronda
half.blurb: A clifftop town split by a deep gorge, connected by the 18th-century Puente Nuevo stone bridge.

half.name: Nerja
half.blurb: A coastal town with the stalactite-filled Nerja Caves and a clifftop promenade called the Balcón de Europa.

half.name: Caminito del Rey
half.blurb: A cliffside walkway of boardwalks and bridges through the Gaitanes Gorge, once one of the world's most dangerous paths.

half.name: Gibraltar
half.blurb: A British overseas territory on a limestone rock, home to wild Barbary macaques and views across the Strait.

half.name: Granada
half.blurb: A city below the Sierra Nevada with the Alhambra palace complex and the old Albaicín quarter's narrow lanes.
